decisions.quote: In a previous study we identified distinct neural contributions to confidence in perceptual detection that were not observed in a performance-matched discrimination task. In this pre-registered follow-up study, we set out to replicate this finding and to further characterize the computational origins of a quadratic modulation of confidence.
decisions.location: discussion (Section 3, line 19); see also Abstract (line 13) and Results (line 15)
decisions.reason: The paper collects new fMRI and behavioural data from a new sample of participants in a pre-registered follow-up experiment to re-test the findings of the authors' previously published 2020 fMRI study [6].

decisions.location: Introduction / Section 1.1 Hypotheses (lines 9-19); Results Section 3.2.6 Hypothesis 6 (line 45); Discussion (line 49); References [6] and [15] (lines 61, 70)
decisions.quote: In our original study [6], a cluster in the rTPJ showed a negative linear effect of confidence, which was significantly more negative in detection ‘no’ compared with ‘yes’ responses. In the current study, activation in this region again showed a negative linear, as well as a positive quadratic effect of confidence. However, an interaction between confidence and detection response was not significant (t34 = 0.72, p = 0.47).
decisions.reason: This paper is an empirical pre-registered fMRI replication of the authors' original 2020 eLife fMRI study [6] (Mazor M, Friston KJ, Fleming SM, 2020, 'Distinct neural contributions to metacognition for detecting, but not discriminating visual stimuli', eLife 9, e53900, DOI 10.7554/eLife.53900), explicitly referred to throughout as 'our original study [6]' and retesting its Hypothesis 6 alongside five hypotheses in the rTPJ, frontopolar cortex, and vmPFC. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 979, DOI 10.1093/nc/niab025) is a separate 2021 behavioural Registered Report by Mazor, Moran, & Fleming in Neuroscience of Consciousness ('Metacognitive asymmetries in visual perception', cited separately as reference [15]), which is not an alternate report of the 2020 eLife fMRI study [6]. Thus, the replicated 2020 eLife study is a genuine missing row.
